doc_summary: Carlini warns AI alignment researchers, using ten years of adversarial ML as a cautionary tale, that looking aligned under natural inputs is easy while worst-case robustness is hard, and that evaluation methods (not just defenses) are the bottleneck. He argues for adversarial, worst-case evaluation and for choosing problems whose success can be checked.

items.claim: Prefers worst-case, adversarial evaluation over observing behavior on natural inputs because models can look aligned when examined naturally while failing under adversarial pressure.
items.quote: you have these models that look like they're aligned when you look at them naturally, but what you actually want is for them to be aligned in some worst-case setting.

items.claim: Prefers an adversary's failure as evidence of safety over random sampling of behavior because if a motivated adversary cannot elicit a behavior, chance occurrence is also unlikely.
items.quote: thinking about the adversarial perspective is a very good way of getting an estimate of the true worst case. If an adversary trying to make something happen cannot succeed, then randomness alone is also not going to make it work.

items.claim: Distrusts published robustness/defense claims that have not been stress-tested by an expert attacker, since top-venue defenses can be broken by trivial changes.
items.quote: Published paper at a top computer security conference, and one character change breaks it. Like 92% clean accuracy, now we're at 5% accuracy under attack.

items.claim: Treats results that run opposite to expectation (attack making the model more accurate) as a red flag for a flawed evaluation, and tests the trivially inverted case to check.
items.quote: I'm following the gradients to make the model get less good, and the model gets more good.” This is somewhat confusing.

items.claim: Prefers problems with a formalizable, automatically checkable objective over fuzzy objectives because without a verifiable metric nobody can tell whether a defense or an elicitation worked.
items.quote: How do you formalize that? What is the mathematical function that is 1 every time the model gives instructions on how to build a bomb, and 0 otherwise? Because if I'm going to try and optimize this, I need some formalism that I can look at.

items.claim: Distrusts claims of success when evaluation relies on humans trying their best, since without automated checks nobody knows whether a defense works.
items.quote: We're going to have a bunch of defenses, no one will know whether or not they worked, and people will just try and be making these claims.

items.claim: Prefers strong, adaptive, optimization-based evaluation over off-the-shelf attacks because running a defense's own attack out of the box can give misleading results.
items.quote: if you run their attack out of the box, what you'll find is that the accuracy goes to 100%.

items.claim: Warns that extrapolating from early progress curves is misleading; reports what the data actually show over time rather than projected trends.
items.quote: it looks like we're making roughly linear progress as we go forward. It kind of looks like you could almost project out into the future and draw a line and say, we'd be at, something like 90% accuracy by now.

items.claim: Prefers choosing a problem whose evaluation is tractable over a nominally easier problem that cannot be evaluated, because an easier-seeming problem is useless if you cannot verify a solution.
items.quote: the problem might be easier, but the evaluation of it is much harder. And so it may be the case that this is an easier problem to solve, but I'm not going to be able to know whether or not you actually have solved it.

items.claim: Toy-looking attacks (cat to guacamole) matter not as realistic threats but because they reveal fundamental failures, so test selection can be driven by what exposes underlying weakness rather than by threat realism.
items.quote: No one is going to turn cats into guacamole. This is not a real threat. But it's pointing to something fundamental for all machine learning models
